claims.text: The protective coating contains both FCC and BCC phases.
The as-deposited coating has a fine, coherent, high-density FCC/BCC interphase-boundary network established by its processing history.
Post-deposition thermal processing can reduce the density or coherence of the FCC/BCC boundaries through coarsening.
Elevated-temperature continuous loading can activate diffusion-controlled creep in the alloy.
Elevated-temperature continuous loading activates dislocation climb in the coating.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries impede dislocation climb.
Coherent FCC/BCC interphase boundaries limit lattice diffusion by acting as physical barriers.
The combined inhibition of dislocation climb and lattice diffusion retards localized strain accumulation and progressive creep.
Deformation is partitioned between the FCC and BCC phases.
Boundary-mediated stress partitioning between the phases slows the steady-state creep rate.
Coatings with a higher density of coherent interphase boundaries will have lower creep strain rates than coatings with fewer or less coherent boundaries.
Coatings with a higher density of coherent interphase boundaries will exhibit a prolonged steady-state creep regime.
Samples retaining dense, coherent boundary networks will resist dislocation motion more effectively.
The proposed boundary mechanism dominates when creep is governed mainly by dislocation climb and lattice diffusion.
At sufficiently extreme temperatures or stresses, phase instability or alternative deformation mechanisms can override the boundary-mediated creep resistance.
The as-deposited dual-phase coating has a characteristic FCC/BCC distribution and established steady-state creep behavior under standard conditions.
Comparing high-boundary-density and thermally coarsened coatings under identical sustained-loading conditions can test the proposed relationship.
Similar or lower creep rates in the reduced-boundary-density group would falsify the claim that coherent boundaries govern creep resistance.
An absence of correlation between measured boundary integrity and creep resistance would falsify the proposed governing role of coherent boundaries.
